title: NASA's Crew-11 Astronauts to Share 167-Day Space Station Saga
summary: After logging 167 days aboard the International Space Station, NASA astronauts Zena Cardman and Mike Fincke, alongside JAXA astronaut Kimiya Yui, are set to share their experiences at a public event on June 1. The talk, part of NASA's Frontiers Forum series, takes place at 11 a.m. EDT at NASA Headquarters in Washington, D.C. Their mission, Expedition 73/74, was a whirlwind of science and maintenance. The crew—which also included Roscosmos cosmonaut Oleg Platonov—traveled nearly 71 million miles and completed over 2,670 orbits of Earth. For Fincke, a veteran with 549 cumulative days in space, this was his fourth flight, placing him fourth among NASA astronauts for total time off-planet. For Cardman and Platonov, it was their first. The mission wasn't just about endurance; it advanced critical research. Experiments conducted on the station aim to improve life on Earth and pave the way for human exploration of the Moon and Mars. A highlight was celebrating the 25th anniversary of continuous human presence on the orbiting lab on November 2, 2025—a milestone underscoring the ISS's role as a unique scientific platform. The crew splashed down off the coast of San Diego on January 15, 2026. While NASA cannot accommodate individual interviews due to the crew's schedule, the public event offers a rare glimpse into life in microgravity. Media must RSVP by 8 a.m. on June 1. For those unable to attend, NASA will share more details about the Frontiers Forum series soon, which focuses on bold thinkers shaping the future of space exploration.
why_it_matters: The experiments the crew ran aboard the ISS are laying the groundwork for future Moon and Mars missions that today’s middle schoolers might one day watch—or even be part of. The public talk gives a rare, direct glimpse into life in space, showing that exploration depends on both science and human endurance.

background_read: The International Space Station (ISS) has been continuously occupied by rotating crews since November 2, 2000, making the 25th anniversary in 2025 a major landmark in human spaceflight.

Zena Cardman, a NASA astronaut with a background in biology and geology, completed her first spaceflight on Expedition 73/74; Mike Fincke is a veteran with four flights and now ranks fourth among NASA astronauts for total cumulative time in space.
Kimiya Yui, a JAXA (Japan Aerospace Exploration Agency) astronaut, previously flew on the ISS in 2015, while Roscosmos cosmonaut Oleg Platonov was also on his first mission.
The crew’s research on materials, medicine and technology in microgravity supports NASA’s Artemis program, which aims to return humans to the Moon and eventually send them to Mars.
Splashdowns off the coast of California are routine for SpaceX Crew Dragon missions; the spacecraft reenters the atmosphere protected by a heat shield before parachuting into the ocean.

perspectives.description: The public event inspires students by letting them hear directly from real-life astronauts, sparking interest in STEM careers. The mission’s research contributes to medical advances, materials science, and space exploration technologies that can improve everyday life on Earth.

Critics point out the ISS is aging and costly to maintain, and that only a handful of astronauts get to fly. The refusal to offer individual interviews may limit deeper public understanding of the crew’s personal experiences and reduce engagement with a wider audience.

The ISS has operated for a quarter century as a model of improbable international cooperation between the U.S., Russia, Japan and other partners. Yet the physical toll of long-duration spaceflight—bone loss, muscle atrophy, radiation exposure—remains a concern as missions push toward Mars.

This crew’s findings may directly influence the design of lunar habitats and spacecraft for NASA’s Artemis program. If NASA expands its Frontiers Forum series, more diverse voices from the space community could reach classrooms and shape how the next generation views space travel.
